claim: Horizontal gene transfer is a driving force behind multidrug-resistance and heightened virulence of healthcare-associated bacterial infections.
source: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a driving force behind the multidrug-resistance and heightened virulence of healthcare-associated bacterial infections (Lerminiaux and Cameron, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genes conferring antibiotic resistance, heightened virulence, and environmental persistence are often encoded on mobile genetic elements.
source: Genes conferring antibiotic resistance, heightened virulence, and environmental persistence are often encoded on mobile genetic elements (MGEs), which can be readily shared between bacterial pathogens via HGT (Juhas, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mobile genetic elements can be readily shared between bacterial pathogens via horizontal gene transfer.
source: Genes conferring antibiotic resistance, heightened virulence, and environmental persistence are often encoded on mobile genetic elements (MGEs), which can be readily shared between bacterial pathogens via HGT (Juhas, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Prior studies have shown that MGEs can mediate and/or exacerbate nosocomial outbreaks.
source: While rates of HGT are not well quantified in clinical settings, prior studies have shown that MGEs can mediate and/or exacerbate nosocomial outbreaks (Bosch et al., 2017; Jamrozy et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Sheppard et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Rates of HGT are not well quantified in clinical settings.
source: While rates of HGT are not well quantified in clinical settings, prior studies have shown that MGEs can mediate and/or exacerbate nosocomial outbreaks (Bosch et al., 2017; Jamrozy et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Sheppard et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Multidrug-resistant healthcare-associated bacteria share MGEs across large phylogenetic distances.
source: Recent studies have also demonstrated that multidrug-resistant healthcare-associated bacteria share MGEs across large phylogenetic distances (Cerqueira et al., 2017; Hazen et al., 2018; Kwong et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Understanding the dynamics of MGE transfer in clinical settings can uncover important epidemiologic links not currently identified by traditional infection control methodologies.
source: Understanding the dynamics of MGE transfer in clinical settings can uncover important epidemiologic links that are not currently identified by traditional infection control methodologies (Lerminiaux and Cameron, 2019; Schmithausen et al., 2019; Stadler et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Methods to identify and track the movement of MGEs among bacterial populations on short timescales are limited.
source: Methods to identify and track the movement of MGEs among bacterial populations on short timescales are limited.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of methodological capabilities in the field.

claim: Bacterial whole-genome sequencing has transformed infectious disease epidemiology over the last decade.
source: Bacterial whole-genome sequencing has transformed infectious disease epidemiology over the last decade (Ladner et al., 2019), providing powerful new tools to identify and intervene against outbreaks (Sundermann et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing provides powerful new tools to identify and intervene against outbreaks.
source: Bacterial whole-genome sequencing has transformed infectious disease epidemiology over the last decade (Ladner et al., 2019), providing powerful new tools to identify and intervene against outbreaks (Sundermann et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Efforts to track MGE movement have focused almost exclusively on drug resistance and virulence genes.
source: Despite these advances, efforts to track MGE movement have focused almost exclusively on drug resistance and virulence genes (Cerqueira et al., 2017; Hardiman et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2017; Stadler et al., 2018), often ignoring the broader genomic context of the mobile elements themselves.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies and describes their limitations.

claim: Previous MGE tracking efforts often ignore the broader genomic context of the mobile elements themselves.
source: Despite these advances, efforts to track MGE movement have focused almost exclusively on drug resistance and virulence genes (Cerqueira et al., 2017; Hardiman et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2017; Stadler et al., 2018), often ignoring the broader genomic context of the mobile elements themselves.
evidence: This statement describes a limitation of prior approaches based on cited literature.

claim: Many studies rely on the identification of plasmid replicons, transposases, and other 'marker genes'.
source: Many studies rely on the identification of plasmid replicons, transposases, and other 'marker genes' (Orlek et al., 2017), an approach that oversimplifies the diversity of MGEs and may lead to incomplete or erroneous conclusions about their epidemiology.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation describing common methodological approaches.

claim: The marker gene approach oversimplifies the diversity of MGEs and may lead to incomplete or erroneous conclusions about their epidemiology.
source: Many studies rely on the identification of plasmid replicons, transposases, and other 'marker genes' (Orlek et al., 2017), an approach that oversimplifies the diversity of MGEs and may lead to incomplete or erroneous conclusions about their epidemiology.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the marker gene approach based on understanding of MGE diversity.

claim: Querying databases containing curated MGE-associated sequences is useful for rapid screening of clinical isolates for known MGEs.
source: While querying databases containing curated MGE-associated sequences is useful for the rapid screening of clinical isolates for known MGEs, it will not capture novel MGEs.
evidence: This statement describes the utility of database-based approaches based on established knowledge.

claim: Database querying will not capture novel MGEs.
source: While querying databases containing curated MGE-associated sequences is useful for the rapid screening of clinical isolates for known MGEs, it will not capture novel MGEs.

claim: Short-read whole-genome sequencing generates genome assemblies that usually do not resolve MGE sequences due to the abundance of repetitive elements.
source: Additionally, whole-genome sequencing using short-read technologies generates genome assemblies that usually do not resolve MGE sequences, due to the abundance of repetitive elements that MGEs often contain (Arredondo-Alonso et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation describing technical limitations of short-read sequencing.

claim: Advances in long-read sequencing can mitigate the problem of resolving MGE sequences.
source: Advances in long-read sequencing can mitigate this problem; hybrid assembly of short- and long-read sequence data allows the genomic context of chromosomal and extrachromosomal MGEs to be precisely visualized (Cerqueira et al., 2017; Conlan et al., 2014; George et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies demonstrating long-read sequencing capabilities.

claim: Hybrid assembly of short- and long-read sequence data allows the genomic context of chromosomal and extrachromosomal MGEs to be precisely visualized.
source: Advances in long-read sequencing can mitigate this problem; hybrid assembly of short- and long-read sequence data allows the genomic context of chromosomal and extrachromosomal MGEs to be precisely visualized (Cerqueira et al., 2017; Conlan et al., 2014; George et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies using hybrid assembly approaches.

claim: Studying the epidemiology of MGEs in clinical settings requires detailed individual-level patient clinical data.
source: Finally, studying the epidemiology of MGEs in clinical settings requires detailed individual-level patient clinical data, without which HGT occurrence in the hospital cannot be identified (Conlan et al., 2014).

source: With this approach, we identified shared sequences that occurred in the genomes of bacteria belonging to different genera.

source: Further analysis using long-read sequencing and reference-based resolution of distinct MGEs enabled us to precisely characterize MGE architecture and cargo, and to track MGE occurrence over time.

claim: The dataset contained 2173 whole-genome sequences of clinical isolates of high-priority Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria collected from a single hospital over an 18-month period beginning in November 2016.
source: To identify genetic material shared between distantly related bacteria in the hospital setting, we screened a dataset containing 2173 whole-genome sequences of clinical isolates of high-priority Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria collected from a single hospital over an 18-month period beginning in November 2016 as part of the Enhanced Detection System for Hospital-Acquired Transmission (EDS-HAT) project at the University of Pittsburgh (Sundermann et al., 2019a) (Methods and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This explicitly describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The isolates were collected as part of the Enhanced Detection System for Hospital-Acquired Transmission (EDS-HAT) project at the University of Pittsburgh.
source: To identify genetic material shared between distantly related bacteria in the hospital setting, we screened a dataset containing 2173 whole-genome sequences of clinical isolates of high-priority Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria collected from a single hospital over an 18-month period beginning in November 2016 as part of the Enhanced Detection System for Hospital-Acquired Transmission (EDS-HAT) project at the University of Pittsburgh (Sundermann et al., 2019a) (Methods and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This explicitly describes the source of the dataset.

claim: An all-by-all alignment of the 2173 genomes was performed using nucmer.
source: We performed an all-by-all alignment of the 2173 genomes in the dataset using nucmer (Marçais et al., 2018), and filtered the results to retain alignments of at least 5 kb that shared 100% identity between bacteria of different genera.
evidence: This describes the computational method used for genome comparison.

claim: Results were filtered to retain alignments of at least 5 kb that shared 100% identity between bacteria of different genera.
source: We performed an all-by-all alignment of the 2173 genomes in the dataset using nucmer (Marçais et al., 2018), and filtered the results to retain alignments of at least 5 kb that shared 100% identity between bacteria of different genera.

claim: Isolates encoding shared sequence clusters were cultured from patients with higher rates of solid organ transplant (p=0.02).
source: While patient demographics were similar between groups, isolates encoding shared sequence clusters were cultured from patients with more co-morbidities (as measured by Charlson co-morbidity index, p=0.03), and with higher rates of solid organ transplant (p=0.02) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing patient groups, with data shown in Table 1.

claim: Shared sequence clusters were often found among bacteria in related genera, in particular the Enterobacteriaceae.

claim: The shared sequences co-occurred in different orders, orientations, and combinations.

claim: The findings support the mosaic, mix-and-match nature of the shorter shared sequences identified.

source: A K. pneumoniae ST405 isolate (KLP00215) and an E. coli ST69 isolate (EC00678) collected from a tissue infection from Patient A each harbored a 113.6 kb IncF plasmid carrying blaKPC-2, blaOXA-9, and blaTEM-1A enzymes, as well as a mercury detoxification operon (Figure 6A,B).

source: Both isolates carried nearly identical 196.8 kb IncF plasmids conferring resistance to aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, chloramphenicol, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, and trimethoprim, as well as operons encoding copper and arsenic resistance (Table 2).

claim: Horizontally-transferred nucleotide sequences found at very high identity within phylogenetically distinct bacteria could be due to recent transfer, optimal adaptation, or high intolerance to mutation.
source: What might cause horizontally-transferred nucleotide sequences to be found at very high identity within phylogenetically distinct bacteria? Among many possible causes, we could consider the following: (1) the sequences we identified could have been recently transferred and not have had time to diverge from one another; (2) they could already be well adapted to optimally perform their functions; or (3) they could represent genetic elements that are highly intolerant to mutation.
evidence: This presents possible explanations for the observed high sequence identity.

claim: The dataset likely contains all three cases of recent transfer, optimal adaptation, and mutation intolerance.
source: We suspect that our dataset contains all three cases.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the diversity of findings.

claim: In instances of likely within-patient HGT, both plasmids isolated from the same patient were nearly identical to one another, suggesting recent transfer.
source: First, in the instances of likely within-patient HGT, both plasmids isolated from the same patient were nearly identical to one another. This suggests that if mutation rates of plasmids are similar to bacterial chromosomes, these plasmids would have transferred shortly before the bacteria were isolated.
evidence: This is an inference about transfer timing based on sequence identity.

claim: If mutation rates of plasmids are similar to bacterial chromosomes, nearly identical plasmids would have transferred shortly before the bacteria were isolated.
